definition: Firmly fixed and hard to change, especially as a habit, belief, or attitude.
example: Years of piano lessons left her with an ingrained habit of counting beats under her breath.
nuance: Ingrained traits are absorbed through long experience, while innate ones are present from birth; ingrained does not mean inborn.
prompt: A coach is trying to fix a swimmer's breathing technique.
options: Ten years of lifting her head to breathe had left the habit ingrained.
The swimmer's ingrained habit appeared on Tuesday and disappeared by Wednesday.
Because the flaw was ingrained, the coach fixed it with a single quick reminder.
The coach had the swimmer's name ingrained on a silver medal after the meet.
reasons: A pattern repeated for a decade becomes settled and resists correction.
Something that comes and goes within a day is fleeting, not deeply rooted.
A deeply settled habit would resist a one-time correction instead of vanishing instantly.
This confuses the word with engraved; letters cut into metal are carved, not fixed habits.

practice.prompt: A family moves from a country where people drive on the left side of the road.
options: Mom's ingrained preference for the left lane faded the moment her plane landed.
The instructor ingrained the family to the local highways during one short lesson.
Their ingrained habit of driving on the left was something they had never once done.
Dad's ingrained reflex kept steering him toward the left lane for weeks.
reasons: A preference that disappears instantly was never deeply rooted to begin with.
The word describes something already fixed; it does not mean to introduce or familiarize.
A habit becomes fixed only through long repetition, so it cannot exist without practice.
An instinct built over many years kept returning even after the rules changed.
